491.title: The greater emptiness
491.hook: a monk who loves company can't find the peace within
491.howItsDone: Many Buddhist monastics and lay meditators set aside periods of solitary retreat, from a day to several years, and monastic codes discourage idle talk about kings, armies and gossip, a list the discourses call 'animal talk'.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a hall empty of elephants, and your line, empty of this. What was your moment empty of? Today, the companion discourse, and a room that's too full. Day four hundred ninety-one.

The Buddha is in his home country, at Kapilavatthu. After his alms round he walks to the dwelling of a Sakyan named Kalakhemaka, and stops. There are beds and mats laid out everywhere. A lot of monks must be living here, he thinks. In fact, Ananda and a group of monks are staying there together, busy making robes. It's useful work. It's also a crowd. The Buddha calls Ananda over. Picture a group chat with forty people in it, buzzing all day, all of it pleasant, none of it quiet. Today: the greater emptiness.
screen: `BEDS LAID OUT EVERYWHERE.` → `ANANDA AND THE MONKS, MAKING ROBES.` → `A FORTY-PERSON GROUP CHAT.`

segments.voice: A monk does not shine, the Buddha tells Ananda, who delights in company, who loves gatherings and being part of a crowd. It's not possible for someone like that to reach, whenever they wish, the ease of seclusion and peace. But someone who lives withdrawn can. Notice he isn't scolding the robe-making. He's talking about where delight lives. Then he describes what he himself does, the abiding he discovered: by not attending to any signs, he enters emptiness within. And he gives the method plainly. First steady the mind inside, quiet it, bring it to one point. Then attend to emptiness inside. If the mind doesn't settle there, attend to emptiness outside, or both, or to stillness. Know honestly whether it's working. And when he does meet visitors, monks, nuns, lay followers, kings and ministers, his mind still leans toward seclusion. He talks with them in a way that sends them off. Then the discourse turns to talk itself. If you must speak, speak of fewness of wishes, contentment, solitude, energy, wisdom. Not of kings and armies and gossip. And at the end, a line about teachers that's worth keeping. I won't treat you, the Buddha says, the way a potter treats damp, unbaked clay, gently. I'll speak pressing and pressing again. What's sound will stand. Space inside isn't loneliness. It's a room in the mind that doesn't depend on who else is in the room. You can carry it into a crowd. But first you build it alone.
screen: `NO SHINE IN LOVING CROWDS` · `STEADY INSIDE, THEN EMPTINESS` · `TALK THAT SENDS PEOPLE OFF` · `PRESSING, PRESSING: WHAT'S SOUND STANDS` · then, large: `SPACE INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: some time alone. The outline asks for one hour alone today, and that's an invitation for later, if your life allows it. For now, two minutes. Turn off what buzzes, if you can. Sit and notice the pull toward company: checking, replying, wondering who's around. Don't fight it. Just feel the space that's here when nobody's talking to you. Let the mind steady inside, then rest in that space. The bell holds the time.
The greater emptiness. The Buddha tells Ananda that love of company blocks the peace of seclusion, and teaches emptiness found within, carried even into crowds. Today's word.
Your line: space inside. Today, find one stretch of time alone, even ten minutes with no screen, and notice what's there when nobody needs you. Day four hundred ninety-one.

options: give up and join the group.
try emptiness outside, or both, and know honestly whether it's working.

fork.reveal: the Buddha gives options: emptiness inside, outside, both, or stillness, always knowing clearly how it's going.

trapdoor: what you thought: emptiness means being alone and lonely.
what it means: a space inside the mind, built in seclusion, that you can carry into any crowd.

492.title: The real marvel
492.hook: Ananda lists the marvels of the birth; the Buddha: here is a marvel, feelings known as they arise
492.howItsDone: Buddhists celebrate the birth of the Buddha at Vesak or, in East Asia, on the Buddha's birthday, often by pouring water over a small statue of the infant Buddha standing with one hand raised, recalling the streams of water in the birth story.

segments.voice: Yesterday: too many beds in one dwelling, and your line, space inside. Did you find a stretch where nobody needed you? Today, a list of wonders, and one more. Day four hundred ninety-two.

Every family has its birth stories. The snowstorm, the taxi, the doctor who almost didn't make it. Told so often they become a kind of legend. In the hundred and twenty-third discourse, monks are sitting together marveling at the Buddha's powers. The Buddha asks Ananda to tell them about the wonderful qualities of a Buddha. And Ananda, who has heard them from the Buddha's own mouth, starts to recite the marvels of his birth. It's a long list. And at the very end, the Buddha adds one of his own. Today: the real marvel.
screen: `THE SNOWSTORM. THE TAXI.` → `ANANDA RECITES THE MARVELS.` → `THE BUDDHA ADDS ONE MORE.`

segments.voice: Ananda's marvels are the great birth story, as this discourse tells it. The one who would become the Buddha passes mindfully from a heavenly realm into his mother's womb, and a great light fills the world, even the dark spaces between worlds. Four young gods guard him. His mother keeps the precepts easily, and can see him within her, the text says, like a thread through a clear gem. She gives birth standing. Gods receive him first. Two streams of water, one cool and one warm, pour from the sky to bathe them. He stands at once, takes seven steps, looks in every direction and declares that this is his last birth. And his mother, the text says, dies seven days later. Ananda tells it all, marvel after marvel, each one ending: this too I remember as a wonderful quality of the Blessed One. Then the Buddha speaks. Then remember this too, Ananda, as a wonderful quality: for the Buddha, feelings are known as they arise, known as they stay, known as they pass. Perceptions too. Thoughts too. That's it. That's the last marvel. After the light across the worlds, after the seven steps, the Buddha points to something that looks almost ordinary: knowing a feeling as it comes and goes. It's the same skill we met with Sariputta, one by one. The birth wonders happen once, to one being. This one is the marvel that the whole path is about, and it can be practiced on an ordinary afternoon.
screen: `A LIGHT ACROSS THE WORLDS` · `SEVEN STEPS, THE LAST BIRTH` · `FEELINGS KNOWN AS THEY ARISE` · `THE MARVEL ANYONE CAN PRACTICE` · then, large: `THE REAL MARVEL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one feeling arise. Sit and settle. Wait for a feeling, not an emotion story, just the tone: pleasant, unpleasant, or neither. An itch. A warm hand. A dull ache. When one appears, know it as it starts. Know it while it stays. Know it as it fades. Then wait for the next. It's small, and that's the point. The bell holds the time.
The real marvel. After Ananda's birth wonders, the Buddha names one more: feelings, perceptions and thoughts, known as they arise, stay and pass. Today's word.
Your line: the real marvel. Today, when something pleasant or painful happens, try to catch the very moment the feeling begins. Day four hundred ninety-two.

options: a marvel of his great powers.

nothing; the list is complete.
fork.reveal: the last marvel is a practice: knowing experience clearly as it comes and goes.

original.note: Pali acchariya: wonderful, a marvel. the discourse's title pairs it with abbhuta, astonishing.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha's greatest marvels are the miracles at his birth.
what it means: the Buddha himself adds one more: feelings and thoughts known clearly as they come and go.
what a scholar hears: MN 123, the Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta, preserves an early birth narrative that later biographies expand, and closes by recasting the marvelous as mindfulness.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 123, Acchariya-abbhuta Sutta (wonderful and marvelous)

493.title: Eighty years in robes
493.hook: the elder Bakkula, eighty years a monk and never ill
493.howItsDone: In Theravada tradition Bakkula is remembered as the monk foremost in good health, and the rag-robe and solitary practices he kept are among the optional ascetic practices (dhutanga) some forest monks still take up today.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the birth marvels, and your line, the real marvel. Did you catch the moment a feeling began? Today, a very old monk, and a visit from an old friend. Day four hundred ninety-three.

An old friend turns up after a lifetime apart, and the first thing out of his mouth is a question nobody else would dare ask. That's how the hundred and twenty-fourth discourse begins. The elder Bakkula is staying near Rajagaha. A naked ascetic named Kassapa, a friend from Bakkula's lay days, comes to see him. How long have you been a monk, friend Bakkula? Eighty years. And then Kassapa asks a blunt personal question about desire. Bakkula doesn't answer it the way it's asked. Today: eighty years in robes.
screen: `AN OLD FRIEND, A LIFETIME LATER.` → `HOW LONG A MONK? EIGHTY YEARS.` → `A BLUNT QUESTION.`

segments.voice: You shouldn't ask it that way, Bakkula says. Ask instead: in eighty years, how many times has a thought of sensual desire even come up? And he answers that one: not once. Then, in the discourse, a long list follows, almost like an inventory of a life. In eighty years, he says, he never accepted a robe from a householder; he wore cast-off cloth. He never sat down to an invitation meal. He never leaned against a wall to rest, never lay down on a bed. And then this: in eighty years, he never had an illness, not even for as long as it takes to pull a cow's teat. He never took so much as a piece of medicinal fruit. On the eighth day after he went forth, he says, he was freed. Each item ends with the same refrain from the reciters: and this too we remember as a wonderful quality of the venerable Bakkula. Kassapa is so moved he asks to go forth under him, and in time reaches the goal himself. Then the ending. One day Bakkula takes a key and goes from dwelling to dwelling, saying: come out, venerables. Today I'll pass away. And he does, sitting among the monks. The Buddha never appears in this discourse. Bakkula's way was unusually strict, and plenty of Buddhists, then and now, take medicine, sit at invitations and wear donated robes. What rings true across eighty years is something simpler: a body used carefully, a life kept plain, and a death met sitting up, among friends.
screen: `ASK IT ANOTHER WAY` · `A PLAIN, EIGHTY-YEAR INVENTORY` · `NEVER ILL, NOT EVEN A MOMENT` · `A KEY, AND A QUIET DEATH` · then, large: `EIGHTY YEARS IN ROBES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank your body today. Bodies are different, and not everyone has Bakkula's health, so this isn't about comparing. Sit and settle. Move your attention slowly through the body. Wherever something is working, a hand that holds, lungs that fill, eyes that read, give it a silent thank you. Where something hurts, just acknowledge it carried you here too. The bell holds the time.
Eighty years in robes. The elder Bakkula, eighty years a monk, never ill even for a moment, who met his death sitting among the monks. Today's word.
Your line: eighty years in robes. Today, do one plain, kind thing for your body: water, a walk, an early night, and notice it as care. Day four hundred ninety-three.

what it means: a plain life, carefully kept, from a reunion question to a death met sitting among friends.

494.title: The wild elephant tamed
494.hook: the mind trained like a forest elephant tied to a post
494.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in many Buddhist traditions describe returning to the breath as gently tying the mind to a post, and Tibetan art often shows taming the mind as an elephant that slowly turns from dark to white along a path.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bakkula's long, plain life, and your line, eighty years in robes. Did you do one kind thing for your body? Today, a much younger monk, and a prince who doesn't believe him. Day four hundred ninety-four.

A young novice named Aciravata is living in a quiet forest hut near Rajagaha. Prince Jayasena comes walking by and asks him a question: is it true that a monk can make the mind truly one-pointed? The novice explains it as best he can. The prince listens, shrugs, says that's impossible, and walks away. Aciravata goes to the Buddha a little crushed. How could a prince who lives for pleasure understand that? the Buddha says. And then he tells a story about elephants. Today: the wild elephant tamed.
screen: `A NOVICE IN THE FOREST.` → `THE PRINCE SAYS: IMPOSSIBLE.` → `THE BUDDHA TELLS AN ELEPHANT STORY.`

segments.voice: First a picture: two friends at the foot of a mountain. One climbs, and from the top sees parks, groves and lakes. The other, still at the bottom, says: what you see is impossible. He's not lying. The mountain is in the way. Then the elephant. A king tells his elephant tamer to go catch a wild forest elephant. The tamer ties a great post into the ground and binds the elephant's neck to it. Why? To wear away its forest habits, its forest memories, its distress at leaving the forest, and to make it comfortable around people. Then he speaks to it gently, words that are pleasant to hear. When the elephant listens, he gives it grass and water. Then simple training: pick this up, put this down. Then harder: stand firm when struck, stay steady in noise. Until at last the elephant is worthy of a king. The Buddha draws the line straight. The posts, he says, are the four foundations of mindfulness. They tie the mind so its old habits, the restless, grasping ones, can wear away. And the gentle words, the food, the small steps, are the training. Even after deep stillness, the Buddha adds one more step: don't think thoughts tied to desire, and later, not even thoughts at all, just rest. Notice the pace. The tamer doesn't beat the elephant. He ties it, talks to it, feeds it, teaches small things first. The mind, in this picture, isn't an enemy. It's a strong, wild creature that can learn, slowly, to stand still.
screen: `THE ONE AT THE FOOT OF THE MOUNTAIN` · `TIED TO A POST, SPOKEN TO GENTLY` · `PICK IT UP, PUT IT DOWN` · `THE POSTS: FOUR FOUNDATIONS` · then, large: `TAMED SLOWLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tie the mind to the breath. Sit, and let the breath be the post. The mind will pull, the way a forest elephant pulls. That's expected. Each time it wanders, bring it back gently, no scolding, just a kind word in your own head, like the tamer's: here. Back to the post. You aren't trying to win. You're getting it used to standing still. The bell holds the time.
The wild elephant tamed. The mind tied to the four foundations of mindfulness like a forest elephant to a post, trained with gentle words and small steps. Today's word.
Your line: tamed slowly. Today, when you catch an old habit pulling at you, speak to yourself the way the tamer spoke: gently, then one small step. Day four hundred ninety-four.

options: leave it alone until it gives up.
speak to it gently, then give food and water when it listens.

fork.reveal: the tamer uses pleasant words, then food and water, then small steps. the training is slow and patient.

original.note: Pali dantabhumi: the tamed state, the ground of the tamed. the title of MN 125.

trapdoor: what you thought: meditation means forcing the mind to stop.
what it means: the mind is tied, spoken to gently and trained in small steps, like a wild elephant.
what a scholar hears: MN 125, the Dantabhumi Sutta, maps the elephant's taming onto the gradual training, with the satipatthanas as the tethering posts and the jhanas beyond.

495.title: Oil from gravel
495.hook: pressing gravel gives no oil, pressing sesame does: right practice bears fruit
495.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often use MN 126 to explain that the path depends on wise method (yoniso) rather than on wishing for results, and sesame oil pressing remains a familiar village craft in South and Southeast Asia.

segments.voice: Yesterday: an elephant tied to a post, and your line, tamed slowly. Did you speak gently to one old habit? Today, the same prince is back, with a new question. Day four hundred ninety-five.

Some people swear by vision boards. Write it down, picture it, want it badly enough, and it comes. Others say wanting is the problem, and you should stop hoping for anything. Prince Jayasena, who doubted the novice yesterday, has heard a version of this argument. He puts it to a monk named Bhumija over a meal at his house. Some teachers say, he tells Bhumija, that whether you hope for results or don't, you won't get them. What does your teacher say? Bhumija isn't sure. So he asks the Buddha. Today: oil from gravel.
screen: `WANT IT BADLY ENOUGH?` → `OR STOP HOPING ALTOGETHER?` → `BHUMIJA TAKES THE QUESTION HOME.`

segments.voice: The Buddha's answer sets the hoping aside. The question isn't whether you wish. It's whether the method fits the goal. Then four pictures, each one a kitchen or farmyard job done wrong and done right. Someone who needs oil fills a tub with gravel, sprinkles it with water, and presses and presses. Hope or no hope, no oil comes. Gravel has none to give. But fill the tub with sesame, sprinkle it, and press: oil comes, whether you hoped for it or not. Someone who wants milk twists a cow's horn. Nothing. Milk the udder: milk. Someone churns water hoping for butter. Nothing. Churn curd: butter. Someone rubs a stick on wet, sappy wood to make fire. Nothing. Use dry wood: fire. So too, the Buddha says, any seeker with wrong view, wrong intention, wrong speech, on through the wrong path, gets no fruit, whether they hope or not. Not because hoping is wrong, but because it's the wrong method. And anyone who practices the eightfold path rightly can reach the fruit, hoping or not. It's surprisingly practical. Hope doesn't make gravel give oil, and indifference doesn't stop sesame from giving it. What matters is what's in the tub. For an ordinary week, that might mean: if a relationship needs listening, more hoping won't do it. If a habit needs sleep, wishing won't make up for it. The Buddha's question is simple and a little blunt: what are you actually pressing?
screen: `NOT WHETHER YOU WISH` · `GRAVEL OR SESAME` · `A HORN, WATER, WET WOOD` · `THE RIGHT PATH BEARS FRUIT` · then, large: `OIL FROM SESAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: try the right way. Sit and settle. Pick one thing you've been pushing at that isn't working: a habit, a conversation, a project. Ask quietly: am I pressing gravel? What would sesame be here? Maybe it's rest instead of effort, or asking instead of guessing. Let one small honest answer show up. Then let it go, and rest with the breath, which is already working. The bell holds the time.
Oil from gravel. Pressing gravel never gives oil, however much you hope; pressing sesame does. The right method bears fruit. Today's word.
Your line: oil from sesame. Today, when something isn't working, stop pressing harder for a moment and check what's in the tub. Day four hundred ninety-five.

options: hope makes the oil come.
no oil comes, hope or no hope.
a little oil comes after a long time.
fork.reveal: gravel has no oil to give. the problem is the method, not the wishing.

original.note: Pali tila: sesame. its oil is tela, and the Sanskrit word for oil, taila, comes from the same root.

trapdoor: what you thought: if you want something enough, you'll get it.
what it means: wanting or not wanting isn't the point; the method has to fit the goal.
what a scholar hears: MN 126, the Bhumija Sutta, answers a debate about asa, hope or expectation, with four paired similes, setting the eightfold path against its wrong counterpart.

496.title: The light fades
496.hook: Anuruddha and his friends lose their inner light; doubt, inattention, fear and more
496.howItsDone: Meditation teachers often use the quail simile from MN 128 to describe balanced effort, and many traditions teach students to notice and name hindrances such as doubt and dullness when concentration falls away.

segments.voice: Yesterday: gravel and sesame, and your line, oil from sesame. Did you check what was really in the tub? Today, three old friends we've met before, and a light that keeps going out. Day four hundred ninety-six.

The hundred and twenty-eighth discourse opens with the Kosambi quarrel, the monks stabbing each other with words. The Buddha tries to make peace, and leaves. He walks alone, and eventually reaches a bamboo park where three monks live: Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila, the ones who live together like milk and water. They tell him how it is: whoever comes back first sets out the seats; whoever sees the water pot empty fills it. Then Anuruddha admits a problem. When we meditate, he says, a light appears, and visions. Then it fades, and we don't know why. Today: the light fades.
screen: `THE QUARREL AT KOSAMBI.` → `THREE FRIENDS, LIKE MILK AND WATER.` → `A LIGHT THAT FADES.`

segments.voice: The Buddha doesn't say the light was nothing. He says: I had this too, before my awakening. I saw light and forms, and they faded, and I had to find out why. Then he lists what he found, the imperfections of the mind, upakkilesa, one at a time. Doubt arose, and the light went. Inattention, and it went. Sleepiness and dullness. Fear, like a traveler who suddenly sees killers jump out on both sides of the road. Elation, like someone looking for one treasure who stumbles on five. Inertia in the body. Then two about effort, and these are the famous ones. Too much energy, like gripping a quail too tightly in your hand: it dies. Too little energy, like holding the quail too loosely: it flies away. Then longing. Then seeing too many different things. Then staring too hard at forms. Eleven in all. Each time, the Buddha says, he understood: this imperfection arose, and because of it my stillness fell away, and the light faded. And each time he resolved: I won't let that arise again. Today's discourse isn't telling anyone to chase lights. It's teaching that when something good fades, there's usually a reason, and the reason can be named. A quail held just right. Effort balanced like a hand that neither crushes nor drops.
screen: `I HAD THIS TOO` · `DOUBT, INATTENTION, FEAR` · `THE QUAIL: TOO TIGHT, TOO LOOSE` · `NAME IT, AND IT CAN BE LEFT` · then, large: `THE LIGHT FADES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one thing that dims you. Sit and settle. Think back over the last day or two to a moment when you felt clear or bright, and then it went. What came in just before? Doubt? Hurry? Too much effort, gripping the quail? Too little, letting it fly? Name it quietly, without blame. Then let the breath be held the way the quail should be: not crushed, not dropped. The bell holds the time.
The light fades. The Buddha tells Anuruddha the inner light fades because of imperfections, like doubt, fear and effort held too tight or too loose, and each can be named. Today's word.
Your line: the light fades. Today, when a good mood slips away, ask what came in just before it, and name that one thing. Day four hundred ninety-six.

match.prompt: why the light fades: tap the pairs.

he says he had it too before his awakening, and teaches why it fades.
MN 128 lists eleven imperfections
from doubt and inattention to effort too tight or too loose and staring too hard at forms.
the three friends quarrel at the start of MN 128

fork.setup: you're holding a quail in your hand. how should you hold it, in the Buddha's picture of effort?
options: tightly, so it can't escape.
loosely, so it's comfortable.
neither too tight nor too loose.
fork.reveal: too tight and it dies; too loose and it flies away. balanced effort is the hand that holds it just right.

original.note: Pali upakkilesa: imperfection, a defilement of the mind. the title of MN 128.

trapdoor: what you thought: if a good feeling in meditation fades, you did something wrong.
what it means: it fades for reasons, doubt, fear, effort too tight or too loose, and each can be named.
what a scholar hears: MN 128 joins the Kosambi narrative to an autobiographical account of the Buddha's own pre-awakening practice with light (obhasa) and forms.

497.title: The fool's three pains
497.hook: the blind turtle again, and the fool who suffers three ways
497.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers across traditions often cite the blind turtle to stress how precious a human birth is, and Tibetan teachings list 'precious human birth' as the first of four thoughts that turn the mind toward practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the quail held too tight or too loose, and your line, the light fades. What came in just before a good mood slipped? Today closes a week. Day four hundred ninety-seven.

You know the feeling. Someone at work mentions, in general, that people have been cutting corners on expenses. They don't look at you. They don't need to. Your face is already hot. The hundred and twenty-ninth discourse is about the fool and the wise person, and it starts with exactly that feeling. A fool, the Buddha says, is someone who thinks badly, speaks badly and acts badly. And such a person doesn't have to wait for any afterlife to suffer. They suffer here, in three ways. Today: the fool's three pains.
screen: `THEY DIDN'T LOOK AT YOU.` → `YOUR FACE IS ALREADY HOT.` → `THREE PAINS, HERE AND NOW.`

segments.voice: Here are the three. First: the fool is sitting in company, and people start talking about the kind of harm he's done. He thinks: they're talking about me. Second: he sees a wrongdoer caught and punished by the king's men, and thinks: that could be me. Third, and this is the image that stays: when he's resting quietly on a chair or a bed, his past wrongs come over him, the text says, the way the shadows of great mountain peaks fall across the land in the evening. Three pains, before anything else happens. The discourse then describes the lower realms after death in vivid, frightening detail, as early Buddhist texts do. And then it returns to an image you met at the start of this year: the blind turtle. A man throws a yoke with a single hole into the ocean. Winds push it east, west, north, south. A blind turtle surfaces once every hundred years. How likely is it that the turtle puts its neck through that hole? The Buddha says that would happen sooner than the fool, once fallen low, regains a human life. Then the bright side, in mirror image. The wise person thinks, speaks and acts well, and has three joys here and now: easy in company, untroubled at the sight of punishment, and at rest in the evening as good deeds fall over them like those same mountain shadows, now cool. Look back at the week: space inside, the real marvel, eighty years in robes, the tamed elephant, sesame and gravel, the light that fades. And now the turtle, surfacing once more.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: value your chance. Sit and settle. Picture the wide ocean, and a small wooden yoke drifting on it. Then remember that you're here: alive, human, with a mind that can listen and change. However today is going, that's rarer than the turtle finding the yoke. Let one breath be a thank you for it. And if a mountain shadow falls over you as you sit, an old regret, just let it be seen, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
The fool's three pains. Fearing they're talked about, fearing they'll be caught, and old wrongs falling over them like mountain shadows at evening. Today's word.
Your line: the turtle and the yoke. Today, use your rare chance on one good act you'd be glad to remember tonight, when the shadows lengthen. Day four hundred ninety-seven.

original.note: Pali bala: fool, literally a child or an immature person. MN 129 sets it against pandita, the wise.
